\vspace*{-6mm}
\begin{center}
{\large\bfseries Speaker Credit History Leaks the Target in LIAR:\\[2pt]
 A Leakage-Free Benchmark for Fine-Grained Fake News Detection}\\[10pt]
{\normalsize Aaron Koshy Parayil}\\[4pt]
{\footnotesize\itshape Department of Computer Science, Christ University,
 Bengaluru 560073, India}\\[3pt]
{\footnotesize E-mail: aaron12parayil@gmail.com}\\[8pt]
\end{center}

\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.4pt}\\[4pt]
{\footnotesize
\noindent\textbf{Abstract}\quad
The LIAR benchmark ships five per-speaker ``credit history'' columns that count
how often a speaker has been rated at each truthfulness level, and a large part
of the published gain from metadata on this dataset is attributed to them. We
show that these columns cannot be used as features as distributed. Measured over
the full corpus, the count vector is constant for 3\,314 of 3\,318 speakers and
equals that speaker's label tally over the training, validation \emph{and} test
splits for 2\,846 of 2\,947 comparable speakers; 1\,689 of 1\,701
single-statement speakers carry a one-hot encoding of their own label. Two
leaks follow: every statement is counted inside its own features, and held-out
labels are visible during training. A random forest given only these five
columns reaches 0.394 six-class test accuracy, and the obvious repair of
subtracting the row's own label makes matters worse, not better, reaching 0.659.
We then rebuild speaker history under three rules --- training labels only,
out-of-fold encoding, and prior smoothing --- which returns the history-only
model to 0.228, just above the 0.208 majority-class rate. On this corrected
footing we benchmark six classical classifiers over three feature modes and two
task granularities under a protocol that selects on validation and scores the
test split once. The best leakage-free configurations reach 0.285 six-class and
0.673 binary test accuracy, with the hybrid feature set beating both
single-modality ablations on both tasks.\\[5pt]
\noindent\textbf{Keywords}\quad credit history, data leakage, fake news
detection, LIAR dataset, text classification\\[2pt]
}
\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.4pt}\\[6pt]
]

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%% ===========================================================================

Misinformation travels faster than the institutions built to correct it. A
single false claim can shape opinion long before a fact-check reaches the
audience that saw it, and the volume of claims produced daily by social
platforms, political speeches and news aggregators far exceeds what any team of
human fact-checkers can verify. That gap between the speed of circulation and
the speed of correction is what motivates automated verification.

Most early work framed the task as binary classification: a statement is either
true or false, and the model sorts one from the other. The framing is convenient
for dataset construction, but it does not match how political statements
actually work. A speaker may state a fact correctly while omitting the context
that changes its meaning; a claim may be accurate in one setting and misleading
in another. Fact-checking organisations recognised this long ago, which is why
PolitiFact rates statements on an ordinal scale --- \emph{true},
\emph{mostly-true}, \emph{half-true}, \emph{barely-true}, \emph{false} and
\emph{pants-fire} --- rather than with a yes-or-no verdict. A system that
collapses that scale is solving an easier and less useful version of the
problem.

The LIAR dataset\cite{wang2017liar} was assembled specifically to keep the
harder version in view. It pairs 12\,836 short PolitiFact statements with their
six-way verdicts and with speaker metadata: party, home state, job title, the
subject tags of the claim, the venue in which it was made, and five integer
columns summarising how often that speaker had previously been rated
\emph{barely-true}, \emph{false}, \emph{half-true}, \emph{mostly-true} and
\emph{pants-fire}. Those last five columns --- the \emph{credit history} --- are
the dataset's distinctive contribution. They encode exactly the kind of
relational, extra-textual context that a bag of words cannot recover from a
twenty-word sentence, and essentially every system that reports a metadata gain
on LIAR consumes them in some form.

This paper starts from an uncomfortable observation about those columns. They
are not a summary of a speaker's \emph{past}. They are a summary of the
speaker's record across the \emph{entire distributed corpus}, computed once and
copied onto every row belonging to that speaker. The consequence is twofold.
First, each statement is counted inside its own feature vector, so the label a
model is asked to predict has already been added to the evidence it is given.
Second, because the same vector is copied onto that speaker's validation and
test rows, held-out labels are visible at training time through a shared
aggregate. Both are textbook target leakage in the sense of Kaufman \emph{et
al.}\cite{kaufman2012leakage}: information about the target that is available to
the model at training time but would not be available at prediction time.

The effect is not subtle. A random forest that sees nothing but the five credit
history columns --- no statement text, no party, nothing else --- reaches 0.394
six-class test accuracy, well above the 0.274 reported for the hybrid
convolutional model introduced with the dataset\cite{wang2017liar}. The obvious
repair, subtracting one from the bucket corresponding to the row's own label,
does not fix the problem: it makes it far worse, lifting the same model to 0.659
accuracy. The reason is instructive and is analysed in Section 3.5. Because the
per-speaker vector is constant and therefore memorisable, subtracting the row's
own label turns the feature vector into an almost injective encoding of that
label.

Correcting this changes what the benchmark says. Once speaker history is rebuilt
so that it uses training labels only, is computed out-of-fold so that no
statement contributes to its own features, and is smoothed toward the corpus
prior so that sparse speakers do not produce saturated vectors, the same
history-only model falls to 0.228 --- barely above the 0.208 majority-class
rate. Speaker history remains a real but modest signal, roughly two accuracy
points rather than nineteen.

\subsection{Contributions}

This paper makes the following contributions.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A quantified leakage audit of LIAR's credit-history columns}
  (Section 3). We characterise the leak structurally --- constancy per speaker,
  agreement with the full-corpus label tally, one-hot self-encoding for
  single-statement speakers --- and measure its effect size with a
  history-only classifier. Every number is produced by a single script in the
  accompanying repository.
\item \textbf{An analysis of why the natural repair fails} (Section 3.5). We
  show that self-exclusion alone is insufficient whenever the aggregate is
  constant per group, and state the condition under which subtracting the row's
  own contribution amplifies rather than removes the leak.
\item \textbf{A leakage-free speaker-history encoder} (Section 4.3) built on
  three rules --- train-only label support, out-of-fold encoding, and
  prior-smoothed proportions --- together with auxiliary features that let a
  model know how much evidence a given history estimate rests on.
\item \textbf{A corrected benchmark} (Section 7) of six classical classifiers
  across three feature modes (text only, metadata only, hybrid) and two task
  granularities, under a protocol that performs all selection on the validation
  split and scores the test split exactly once. We report accuracy, macro-F1
  and weighted-F1 with interval estimates, and we give per-class results and a
  confusion analysis for the strongest configuration.
\item \textbf{Practical guidance} (Section 8.4) for future work on LIAR: what
  to do with the shipped columns, what a defensible metadata baseline looks
  like, and which published comparisons are and are not safe to make.
\end{itemize}

We deliberately restrict the model family to classical, fully reproducible
classifiers. The point of the paper is the measurement protocol, not a new
architecture; introducing a transformer or a speaker graph at the same time as
the corrected features would make it impossible to attribute any change to the
correction. Section 9 sets out how those extensions should consume the corrected
history when they are added.

\subsection{Organisation}

Section 2 reviews related work across the paradigms that have been applied to
LIAR and positions this paper among them. Section 3 describes the dataset and
presents the leakage audit. Section 4 describes the corrected pipeline.
Section 5 gives the experimental setup, Section 6 the exploratory analysis, and
Section 7 the results. Section 8 discusses what the corrected numbers mean for
the literature and states the limitations of the study. Section 9 concludes.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Why Binary Framing Falls Short}

Most early work in this area treated fake news detection as a two-class problem.
The framing simplifies dataset construction, but it does not survive contact
with how fact-checkers operate: a statement is rarely simply true or false, and
where it falls on the scale often depends on material outside the sentence ---
who said it, what they meant, and what was omitted. Producing that judgment is a
different and considerably harder problem than binary classification, and it is
the problem LIAR was designed to expose. The distinction matters when reading
reported accuracies: binary numbers above 0.90 on corpora such as WELFake are
routinely quoted alongside six-way numbers below 0.50 on LIAR, and the two are
not measuring the same difficulty.

\subsection{Feature-Based Models and Their Ceiling}

LIAR was introduced to move the field past binary
labels\cite{wang2017liar}: roughly 12\,800 statements rated on a six-point
scale, with speaker metadata attached. Standard models --- support vector
machines, logistic regression, and a simple convolutional network --- reached
around 0.27 six-way accuracy, which says less about those models than about the
difficulty of the task once the label space is no longer binary. A follow-up
approach supplied the fact-checkers' written justifications alongside the
statement and trained a bidirectional LSTM, reaching roughly
0.36\cite{alhindi2018where}. That is a substantial jump, but the justification
text is written \emph{after} the verdict, so a system that consumes it is not
performing the same task as one that must decide from the claim and its context
alone. This is worth naming explicitly, because it is the same category of
problem as the one we document for the credit-history columns: a feature that
encodes the answer produces an impressive number and a useless model. Elsewhere,
a CNN--LSTM applied to Hindi-language news reported very high accuracy within
that language\cite{gupta2025fake}, though transfer to other languages and
domains was not established.

\subsection{Modelling Speakers as a Network}

A statement does not exist in isolation, and several lines of work have tried to
capture who is speaking. One approach builds a graph over speakers, parties and
statements and frames detection as node classification with a relational graph
neural network\cite{kirilin2019relational}, improving on text-only baselines to
roughly 0.38 but degrading on speakers absent from the graph --- a common
deployment scenario, and one the LIAR splits themselves exhibit, since 15.6\% of
test statements come from speakers with no training-set history at all.
A later approach combined a transformer with a graph convolutional network and
contrastive learning, reporting close to 0.46\cite{park2024graph} at the cost of
substantial graph-construction overhead. A co-attention GNN over user profiles
reported much higher figures on GossipCop and PolitiFact\cite{khedairia2025co},
but those corpora are structured differently from LIAR and the numbers are not
directly comparable.

\subsection{Transformers}

Once attention-based encoders became standard, several groups applied them
directly. Fine-tuned BERT reached roughly 0.41 six-way accuracy on
LIAR\cite{khan2020fake}; the 512-token limit is not a binding constraint for
statements averaging eighteen words, so the remaining difficulty is contextual
rather than lexical. Folding metadata in through dual attention and an MLP
fusion layer reached about 0.435\cite{yang2022multimodal}, with sensitivity to
missing metadata fields --- relevant here, since job title and state are absent
for 27.9\% and 21.5\% of LIAR rows respectively.

\subsection{Large Language Models and Efficient Fine-Tuning}

As models grew, the question shifted from representation quality to adaptation
cost. Prompt and prefix tuning on GPT-2 avoided full
retraining\cite{zhou2023fine} but proved sensitive to prompt wording.
DeBERTa-v3 gave a further increase to roughly 0.47\cite{martinez2024deberta} at
higher compute cost. LLaMA-2 and Mistral were evaluated in few-shot settings
without fine-tuning\cite{kumar2024combating}, with five-shot prompting reaching
about 0.46 at high inference cost. The strongest reported results combine large
pretrained encoders with efficient fine-tuning: around 0.48 six-way accuracy and
close to 0.90 binary accuracy across BERT, RoBERTa and
DeBERTa\cite{alqadi2025transfer}, a comparable gain from LoRA on
Mistral-7B\cite{thompson2025parameter}, and binary accuracy above 0.99 with
lightweight adapters\cite{alghamdi2025abert} --- the last on a binary corpus,
which as noted above is a different problem. A mixture-of-experts arrangement on
LLaMA-3.1 that routes text and metadata through different experts reported
roughly 0.49\cite{garcia2026hybrid}, requiring multi-GPU infrastructure.

\subsection{Generalisation, Explainability and Robustness}

Beyond raw accuracy, three practical issues recur. Cross-dataset transfer is
weak, and domain-adversarial training has been used to recover a cross-domain
F1 near 0.74\cite{patel2025cross}. Explainability has been approached with
attribution methods layered over DeBERTa\cite{nguyen2025explaining}, which
matters if such systems are to be trusted operationally. Robustness to
deliberate manipulation remains open; adversarial training against
GPT-4o-generated attacks held up only
partially\cite{almansoori2025adversarial}. Self-supervised pretraining has been
explored to reduce label dependence\cite{sun2026self}, and temporal drift ---
the degradation of a model as political discourse moves --- has been studied
directly\cite{oconnor2026temporal}, a failure mode invisible in a static
benchmark.

\subsection{Leakage and Evaluation Hygiene}

The methodological literature this paper leans on is older and largely outside
misinformation research. Kaufman \emph{et al.}\cite{kaufman2012leakage} give the
standard formulation of leakage as the introduction of information about the
target that would not legitimately be available at prediction time, together
with the observation that leakage is usually discovered through implausibly good
results rather than through code review. Out-of-fold construction of
target-derived features, and smoothing of per-category statistics toward a
global prior, are standard practice for high-cardinality categorical
encoding\cite{miccibarreca2001preprocessing}; the encoder in Section 4.3 is an
application of that technique to a leak that happens to be baked into a
published file rather than introduced by the modeller. On the evaluation side,
Gorman and Bedrick\cite{gorman2019standard} show that conclusions drawn from a
single standard split are frequently not reproduced under resampling, and Dodge
\emph{et al.}\cite{dodge2019show} show that reported test numbers are
uninterpretable without the size of the search that produced them. Both
directly inform the protocol in Section 4.7.

\subsection{Positioning}

Table~\ref{tab:positioning} summarises where this work sits. The lineage above
is a story of increasing model capacity on a fixed benchmark. This paper asks a
prior question --- whether the benchmark's metadata can be used at all as
distributed --- and finds that it cannot. The contribution is therefore not a
competitive accuracy number; on the corrected footing no classical model is
competitive with a fine-tuned encoder, and we do not claim otherwise. It is a
corrected measurement protocol, a corrected feature construction, and a set of
reference numbers that later systems can be compared against without inheriting
the leak.

\section{The LIAR Corpus and a Leakage Audit of Its Credit History}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Corpus and Fields}

LIAR\cite{wang2017liar} distributes 12\,836 short statements collected from
PolitiFact as three headerless tab-separated files. Each row carries fourteen
fields: a statement identifier, the six-way verdict, the statement text, a
comma-separated list of subject tags, the speaker's name, job title, home state
and party, five integer credit-history counts, and the venue or context in which
the statement was made. Table~\ref{tab:fields} lists them with their cardinality
and missingness over the combined corpus.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Fields of the LIAR corpus, measured over all 12\,836 rows}
\label{tab:fields}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrr@{}}
\toprule
Field & Type & Distinct & Missing \\
\midrule
\texttt{id}            & identifier   & 12\,836 & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{label}         & ordinal, 6 levels & 6  & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{statement}     & free text    & 12\,810 & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{subject}       & multi-label tags & 144 tags & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{speaker}       & categorical  & 3\,318 & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{job\_title}    & categorical  & 1\,348 & 27.86\% \\
\texttt{state}         & categorical  & 70     & 21.46\% \\
\texttt{party}         & categorical  & 24     & 0.00\% \\
\texttt{context}       & categorical  & 5\,080 & 1.00\% \\
\texttt{*\_c} (five columns) & integer counts & 392 vectors & 0.00\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: distinct values are counted after whitespace
normalisation; missingness is measured before imputation. \texttt{subject} holds
4\,547 distinct comma-separated combinations built from 144 atomic tags. The
five credit-history columns are treated as a single vector here; only 392
distinct vectors occur across 3\,318 speakers. The one-hot blocks of
Table~\ref{tab:blocks} use only the categories present in the training split
(23 parties, 70 states).}
\end{table}

The six verdicts form an ordinal scale, from \emph{pants-fire} (a fabrication)
through \emph{false}, \emph{barely-true}, \emph{half-true} and
\emph{mostly-true} to \emph{true}. We keep the dataset's own split into 10\,269
training, 1\,284 validation and 1\,283 test statements, both because it is the
comparison point used by every published result on this corpus and because
re-splitting would obscure the cross-split structure that the audit below is
about. Table~\ref{tab:splits} gives the label distribution per split.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Label distribution across the official LIAR splits}
\label{tab:splits}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Label & Train & Valid & Test & Corpus \\
\midrule
\emph{pants-fire}  &   842 & 116 &  92 & 1\,050 \;(8.18\%) \\
\emph{false}       & 1\,998 & 263 & 250 & 2\,511 \;(19.56\%) \\

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: the true-leaning share is the positive rate of the binary
task, in which \{\emph{half-true}, \emph{mostly-true}, \emph{true}\} are
collapsed into one class and the remaining three into the other.}
\end{table}

Five of the six classes occupy a narrow band between 16\% and 21\% of the
corpus; only \emph{pants-fire} is markedly rarer at 8.18\%. Unlike many binary
misinformation corpora, LIAR therefore does not demand aggressive resampling to
prevent a model from collapsing onto a majority class --- but the 0.2081
majority rate on the test split is also a reminder of how little headroom a
six-way accuracy figure actually has.

\subsection{What the Credit-History Columns Contain}

The five credit-history columns are described in the dataset's documentation as
the speaker's total credit history counts, excluding the current statement. We
examine that claim directly. Write $\mathcal{L}$ for the six labels and
$\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{L}\setminus\{\textsc{true}\}$ for the five labels that
actually have a column --- there is no \texttt{true\_c} bucket, an asymmetry
that turns out to matter. For statement $i$ let $s(i)$ be its speaker, $y_i$ its
label, and $\bs{b}_i \in \mathbb{N}^{5}$ its shipped count vector. Let
$\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\text{va}} \cup
\mathcal{D}_{\text{te}}$ be the full corpus.

\begin{definition}[Self-inclusion]
A feature map $\phi$ is \emph{self-including} if $\phi(i)$ depends on $y_i$.
Any such feature is unavailable at prediction time, since $y_i$ is what is being
predicted.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cross-split aggregation]
A feature map is \emph{cross-split aggregating} if $\phi(i)$ for a training row
$i$ depends on $\{y_j : j \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{va}} \cup
\mathcal{D}_{\text{te}}\}$. Any such feature transports held-out labels into
training.
\end{definition}

The audit is implemented in \texttt{scripts/leakage\_analysis.py} and reports
the quantities in Table~\ref{tab:audit}.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Structural audit of the shipped credit-history columns}
\label{tab:audit}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Property & Measurement \\
\midrule
Count vector is constant per speaker & 3\,314 / 3\,318 \\
Counts equal the speaker's tally over & \multirow{2}{*}{2\,846 / 2\,947} \\
\quad train $\cup$ valid $\cup$ test & \\
Single-statement speakers whose counts & \multirow{2}{*}{1\,689 / 1\,701} \\
\quad one-hot encode their own label & \\
\emph{true}-labelled single-statement speakers & \multirow{2}{*}{355 / 355} \\
\quad with an all-zero count vector & \\
Distinct count vectors across the corpus & 392 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: the second row compares only the 2\,947 speakers for whom
the comparison is well defined; \emph{true} statements are excluded from the
tally because no \texttt{true\_c} column exists.}
\end{table}

Three facts follow from the table.

\textbf{The vector is a per-speaker constant.} For 3\,314 of 3\,318 speakers,
every row belonging to that speaker carries an identical count vector. The
columns are therefore not a running, statement-by-statement history; they are a
single aggregate broadcast onto every row.

\textbf{The aggregate spans all three splits.} For 2\,846 of the 2\,947
speakers where the comparison is well defined, the shipped vector equals that
speaker's label histogram computed over the training, validation \emph{and} test
files combined. A training row belonging to a speaker who also appears in the
test split therefore carries, in its features, a summary that counts that
speaker's test labels.

\textbf{The current statement is inside its own features.} The clearest case is
a speaker with exactly one statement in the corpus. Then the aggregate has a
single unit in it, and that unit is the row's own label.

\begin{proposition}[Exact recovery for single-statement speakers]
\label{prop:solo}
Let $s$ have exactly one statement $i$ in $\mathcal{D}$, and suppose
$\bs{b}_i$ equals $s$'s corpus tally. Then
$\bs{b}_i = \bs{e}_{y_i}$ if $y_i \in \mathcal{C}$, and $\bs{b}_i = \bs{0}$ if
$y_i = \textsc{true}$. In either case $y_i$ is a deterministic function of
$\bs{b}_i$.
\end{proposition}

Empirically, 1\,689 of 1\,701 single-statement speakers with a non-\emph{true}
label carry exactly $\bs{e}_{y_i}$, and all 355 single-statement \emph{true}
speakers carry the zero vector. That is 2\,044 of 2\,056 rows --- 16\% of the
corpus --- whose label is readable straight off the feature vector. Note the
second clause: because \emph{true} has no bucket, the all-zero vector is not a
neutral ``no history'' signal but a positive indicator of a \emph{true} label
among single-statement speakers, which is precisely the kind of encoding a
gradient-boosted or tree-based learner will find immediately.

\subsection{Two Worked Examples}

The abstractions above are easier to see in two actual rows of the corpus.

\textbf{Self-inclusion.} The very first row of \texttt{train.tsv} belongs to
speaker \texttt{dwayne-bohac}, carries the label \emph{false}, and has the count
vector $(0,1,0,0,0)$ in the column order
(\texttt{barely\_true}, \texttt{false}, \texttt{half\_true},
\texttt{mostly\_true}, \texttt{pants\_fire}). This speaker has exactly one
statement in the entire corpus. The single unit in the vector is that statement.
A model reading the second coordinate of the first training row is reading its
label, and no amount of model-side regularisation changes that.

\textbf{Cross-split aggregation.} Speaker \texttt{john-edwards} has fifteen
statements: twelve in training, two in validation and one in test. Every one of
those fifteen rows carries the identical vector $(0,2,4,4,1)$, which is the
speaker's tally over the whole corpus. The training rows alone would give
$(0,1,4,4,0)$. The difference is exactly the two validation statements --- one
\emph{false} and one \emph{pants-fire} --- whose labels are therefore visible,
in aggregate, inside the features of twelve training rows. The test statement is
labelled \emph{true} and contributes nothing, because no \texttt{true\_c} bucket
exists; had it been labelled anything else, a test label would have been visible
during training in the same way.

Neither example depends on an unusual speaker. The first is the first row of the
file, and the second is an ordinary politician with an ordinary number of
fact-checks.

\subsection{Effect Size}

Structure alone does not tell us how much accuracy the leak manufactures, so we
measure it. A random forest (100 trees, maximum depth 25, seed 42) is given
\emph{only} the five count columns --- no statement text, no party, no state ---
and evaluated on the six-class task. Table~\ref{tab:effect} and
Fig.~\ref{fig:leakage} report the result under four feature constructions.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{History-only random forest on the six-class task, under four
constructions of the same underlying signal}
\label{tab:effect}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Construction & Test acc. & Macro-F1 \\
\midrule
Raw LIAR counts (as shipped)   & 0.3944 & 0.4056 \\
Naive repair $\bs{b} - \bs{e}_y$ & 0.6594 & 0.6633 \\
Leak-free out-of-fold history  & 0.2284 & 0.2236 \\
\midrule
Majority class                 & 0.2081 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: the first two rows are diagnostics, not performance
estimates. Neither construction could be computed at prediction time for an
unseen statement.}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_leakage.pdf}
\caption{Six-class test accuracy of a random forest given only speaker credit
history, under four constructions of that history. The dashed line is the
majority-class rate. The first two bars are leaking constructions and are shown
to quantify the leak, not as performance estimates}
\label{fig:leakage}
\end{figure}

Five columns of integers, with no access to what was actually said, reach 0.3944
--- nearly double the majority rate, and well above the 0.274 originally
reported for a hybrid convolutional model that used the statement text as
well\cite{wang2017liar}. That gap is the signature Kaufman \emph{et
al.}\cite{kaufman2012leakage} describe: a result too good for the information
nominally available.

\subsection{Why the Naive Repair Makes It Worse}
\label{sec:naive}

The obvious correction is to remove the current statement's own contribution:
replace $\bs{b}_i$ with $\bs{b}'_i = \max(\bs{b}_i - \bs{e}_{y_i},\bs{0})$ for
$y_i \in \mathcal{C}$, leaving \emph{true} rows untouched. The second row of
Table~\ref{tab:effect} shows what happens: accuracy rises from 0.3944 to 0.6594.
The repair does not remove the leak, it sharpens it.

The mechanism is worth stating precisely, because the same trap recurs whenever
a group-level aggregate is self-inclusive.

\begin{proposition}[Self-exclusion from a constant aggregate is invertible]
\label{prop:naive}
Suppose the aggregate $\bs{B}_s$ is constant across all rows of speaker $s$ and
observable from the training split, and let
$\bs{b}'_i = \bs{B}_{s(i)} - \bs{e}_{y_i}$. If $\bs{B}_{s(i)}$ can be recovered
from $\bs{b}'_i$ --- in particular whenever $\bs{b}'_i + \bs{e}_c$ is an
observed aggregate for exactly one $c \in \mathcal{C}$ --- then $y_i$ is
determined by $\bs{b}'_i$.
\end{proposition}

\noindent In other words, subtracting the label makes the feature vector a
\emph{displacement} from a memorisable landmark, and the direction of the
displacement is the label. The premise holds here: there are only 392 distinct
count vectors across 3\,318 speakers, all of them observable in the training
split, so the landmark set is small enough for a tree ensemble to memorise
outright. Measuring the consequence directly on the test split, the repaired
vector determines the label exactly for 464 of 1\,283 rows (36.2\%), and the
mean number of labels consistent with a repaired vector is 3.61 out of six.
Exact recovery on a third of the split, plus a narrowed candidate set on much of
the remainder, is enough to explain why a model that should have been weakened
by the repair is instead twice as accurate.

The practical lesson generalises beyond LIAR: \emph{self-exclusion is not
sufficient when the aggregate is constant within a group}. The row's own
contribution must be removed at a granularity coarser than the row --- a fold,
in the construction of Section 4.3 --- so that the residual does not point back
at the removed item.

\subsection{Diagnosis}

The credit-history columns fail both definitions above at once. They are
self-including, so a model is shown the answer; and they are cross-split
aggregating, so a model is shown the held-out answers too. Any published result
that consumes them as distributed is measuring, to an unknown extent, a model's
ability to read its own labels. We are not in a position to say which published
systems are affected: papers reporting metadata gains on LIAR rarely state how
these columns were handled, and the effect depends on whether they were fed in
raw, aggregated, or dropped. What we can say is that the columns are unusable
without reconstruction, that reconstruction must be more careful than
subtracting the row's own label, and that the corrected signal is far weaker
than the raw columns suggest --- roughly two accuracy points over the majority
class rather than nineteen.

The rest of this paper takes that correction as its starting point.
%% ===========================================================================
\section{Method}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Overview}

Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline} shows the pipeline. It is deliberately asymmetric across
splits: every step that consumes labels is fitted on the training split alone,
and the one step that consumes labels \emph{and} is applied back to the training
split --- speaker history --- is applied out-of-fold. Everything upstream of
that is split-local, meaning it can be computed for a single row in isolation
and therefore cannot leak by construction.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/fig_pipeline.pdf}
\caption{End-to-end pipeline. Shaded blocks are the three stages where the
design differs from a conventional LIAR pipeline: label-derived speaker
features are built out-of-fold from training labels only, the feature union
excludes the shipped count columns, and all selection happens on the validation
split}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Preprocessing}

\textbf{Loading.} The three files are read with no header and with quoting
disabled, since statement text contains unbalanced quotation marks that a naive
parser silently merges into neighbouring records. Each split is tagged with its
origin so that the partition can be recovered after any concatenation.

\textbf{Cleaning.} Every object column is stripped of leading and trailing
whitespace, and the strings \texttt{""}, \texttt{"nan"} and \texttt{"None"} are
normalised to true missing markers. This matters more than it appears: an empty
string is not missing as far as \texttt{pandas} is concerned, so omitting the
step causes every subsequent missingness count to be wrong.

\textbf{Deduplication.} Duplicates are removed on \texttt{id} only. There are
none. Twenty-six statements share their text with another row, and these are
retained: politicians repeat talking points across appearances, and those are
distinct fact-checked records, not database duplicates.

\textbf{Null handling.} Rows missing a core field (\texttt{label},
\texttt{statement}, \texttt{party}) are dropped; none are. High-missingness
metadata (\texttt{job\_title}, \texttt{state}, \texttt{context},
\texttt{subject}, \texttt{speaker}) is imputed with an explicit
\texttt{"Unknown"} category rather than discarded, so that a row with a usable
statement and label is not lost because one metadata field is absent. Treating
absence as its own category also lets a model learn from the absence itself,
which is informative here: missing job title and state correlate with speakers
who are organisations, media outlets or social-media posts rather than
individual officeholders.

\textbf{Text statistics.} Three surface features are computed per statement:
character length, word count, and mean word length (characters divided by
words). These are split-local and cheap, and Section 6 shows they are close to
uncorrelated with speaker history, so they contribute independent signal.

\textbf{Label encoding.} The six-way target is mapped to
$\{0,\dots,5\}$ in order of increasing truthfulness. The binary target
collapses $\{$\emph{half-true}, \emph{mostly-true}, \emph{true}$\}$ against
$\{$\emph{pants-fire}, \emph{false}, \emph{barely-true}$\}$, giving a
0.5666 majority rate on test. We state this explicitly because the binary
collapse is not standardised in the literature: a two-way split at
\emph{mostly-true} instead yields a different majority rate and different
numbers, and the two are frequently quoted against each other.

\subsection{Leakage-Free Speaker Credit History}
\label{sec:leakfree}

The shipped columns are discarded entirely for modelling purposes --- they are
retained in the processed files only so that the audit of Section 3 can be
reproduced --- and speaker history is rebuilt from scratch under three rules.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Train-only support.} Only training labels ever enter any feature,
  so validation and test labels are never observed, directly or in aggregate.
\item \textbf{Out-of-fold encoding.} Training rows are encoded from the
  training rows \emph{outside their own fold}, so no statement contributes to
  its own features, and --- by Proposition~\ref{prop:naive} --- the residual
  does not point back at what was removed.
\item \textbf{Prior smoothing.} Counts become proportions shrunk toward the
  global training prior, so a speaker with one prior statement does not produce
  a saturated, memorisable vector.
\end{enumerate}

Formally, let $\hat{\bs{p}} \in \Delta^{5}$ be the training label distribution
over all six labels --- note that, unlike the shipped columns, \emph{true} gets
a bucket here --- and let
\begin{equation}
\bs{n}_s \;=\; \sum_{j \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}},\, s(j)=s} \bs{e}_{y_j}
\end{equation}
be speaker $s$'s training label histogram. Partition
$\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$ into $K=5$ stratified folds
$F_1,\dots,F_K$ and write $\bs{n}_s^{(k)}$ for the histogram restricted to fold
$k$. The count vector assigned to row $i$ is
\begin{equation}
\bs{c}_i \;=\;
\begin{cases}
\max\!\left(\bs{n}_{s(i)} - \bs{n}_{s(i)}^{(k(i))},\, \bs{0}\right),
 & i \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}},\\[4pt]
\bs{n}_{s(i)}, & i \notin \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}},
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $k(i)$ is the fold containing $i$. With $T_i = \|\bs{c}_i\|_1$ and
smoothing strength $m = 10$, the history features are the shrunken proportions
\begin{equation}
\bs{\pi}_i \;=\; \frac{\bs{c}_i + m\,\hat{\bs{p}}}{T_i + m},
\label{eq:smooth}
\end{equation}
which is the standard smoothed target encoding for high-cardinality categorical
variables\cite{miccibarreca2001preprocessing}. Equation~(\ref{eq:smooth})
interpolates between the speaker's own record and the corpus prior as a function
of how much evidence there is: at $T_i = 0$ it returns the prior exactly, and it
reaches the halfway point at $T_i = m = 10$ prior statements.

Three auxiliary features accompany the proportions, all of which describe the
\emph{reliability} of the estimate rather than its content: the support $T_i$
enters as $\log(1+T_i)$, an indicator $\mathbf{1}[T_i = 0]$ marks speakers with
no usable history, and a single ordinal summary
\begin{equation}
\text{cred}_i \;=\; \bs{\pi}_i^{\!\top} \bs{w},\quad
\bs{w} = (-3,\,-2,\,-1,\,0.5,\,1,\,2)^{\!\top}
\end{equation}
collapses the distribution into a scalar in $[-3,2]$ ordered from fabrication to
truth. The indicator matters: 15.6\% of test statements and 17.2\% of validation
statements come from speakers with no training history at all, and without the
flag a model cannot distinguish ``this speaker has a prior record centred on the
corpus average'' from ``we know nothing about this speaker''.

Algorithm~\ref{alg:history} states the procedure. Speaker keys are lowercased
and trimmed, and the placeholder values \texttt{unknown}, \texttt{nan},
\texttt{none} and the empty string are mapped to the null key so that
unattributed statements are not pooled into one artificial mega-speaker.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Leakage-free speaker credit history}
\label{alg:history}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require training split $\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$, target split $\mathcal{D}$,
 folds $K$, smoothing $m$
\State $\hat{\bs{p}} \gets$ label distribution of $\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$
\State $\bs{n}_s \gets$ label histogram of speaker $s$ over
 $\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$, for all $s$
\If{$\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$}
  \State assign stratified folds $F_1,\dots,F_K$ over $\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$
  \For{$k = 1$ \textbf{to} $K$}
    \State $\bs{n}^{(k)}_s \gets$ histogram of $s$ restricted to $F_k$
    \For{$i \in F_k$}
      \State $\bs{c}_i \gets \max(\bs{n}_{s(i)} - \bs{n}^{(k)}_{s(i)}, \bs{0})$
    \EndFor
  \EndFor
\Else
  \For{$i \in \mathcal{D}$}
    \State $\bs{c}_i \gets \bs{n}_{s(i)}$ \quad ($\bs{0}$ if $s(i)$ unseen)
  \EndFor
\EndIf
\For{$i \in \mathcal{D}$}
  \State $T_i \gets \|\bs{c}_i\|_1$
  \State $\bs{\pi}_i \gets (\bs{c}_i + m\hat{\bs{p}})/(T_i + m)$
  \State emit $\bs{\pi}_i$, $\log(1+T_i)$, $\mathbf{1}[T_i = 0]$,
   $\bs{\pi}_i^{\!\top}\bs{w}$
\EndFor
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{proposition}[The encoder is neither self-including nor cross-split
aggregating]
\label{prop:safe}
For $i \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$, $\bs{c}_i$ is a function of
$\{y_j : j \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}} \setminus F_{k(i)}\}$, a set that
excludes $i$. For $i \notin \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}$, $\bs{c}_i$ is a function
of $\{y_j : j \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}\}$, a set that also excludes $i$. In
neither case does any validation or test label appear.
\end{proposition}

Two honest caveats follow from the construction. First, training rows see
roughly $(K-1)/K = 80\%$ of the available history while held-out rows see all of
it, a mild distribution shift that the support feature $\log(1+T_i)$ is there to
expose. Second, a training row's features do depend on the labels of
\emph{other} statements by the same speaker; that is the intended signal, not a
leak, and it is exactly what a deployed system would have --- a record of what
the speaker has previously been rated.

\subsection{Feature Representation}

Five feature blocks are concatenated into a single sparse matrix.
Table~\ref{tab:blocks} lists them.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Feature blocks and their dimensionality under the default
configuration}
\label{tab:blocks}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
\toprule
Block & Construction & Dim. \\
\midrule
Word TF-IDF   & 1--2 grams, sublinear tf, & 5\,000 \\
              & \;\;min\_df 2, max\_df 0.95, & \\
              & \;\;English stop words & \\
Char TF-IDF   & \texttt{char\_wb} 3--5 grams, & 20\,000\rlap{$^\dagger$} \\
              & \;\;min\_df 3 & \\
Numeric       & 6 history proportions, cred., & 12 \\
              & \;\;$\log$ support, unseen flag, & \\
              & \;\;3 text statistics ($z$-scored) & \\
One-hot       & \texttt{party} (23), \texttt{state} (70) & 93 \\
Subject       & TF-IDF over comma-split tags & 140 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{Total, hybrid mode (default)} & 5\,245 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: $^\dagger$character n-grams are off in the default
configuration and are treated as a binary choice during model selection
(Section 4.7). The one-hot block grows to 4\,000--9\,000 columns when
\texttt{speaker}, \texttt{job\_title} and \texttt{context} are enabled.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Word TF-IDF} over unigrams and bigrams with sublinear term-frequency
scaling\cite{salton1988term}, a vocabulary capped at 5\,000, a minimum document
frequency of 2 and a maximum of 0.95, with English stop words removed.

\textbf{Character TF-IDF} over 3- to 5-grams within word boundaries, capped at
20\,000 features. Character n-grams are robust to the morphological variation
and proper-noun density of political speech, and the search in Section 7.4
selects them for most configurations.

\textbf{Numeric features}, $z$-scored with a scaler fitted on the training split
and applied unchanged to the held-out splits. Min--max variants are also
computed and stored, so that a downstream model with different requirements can
use them without re-deriving the pipeline.

\textbf{One-hot metadata} for categorical fields, with unseen categories at
transform time mapped to all-zero rather than raising --- necessary because the
test split contains states and parties absent from training.

\textbf{Subject tags}, which are multi-label in LIAR
(\texttt{"energy,history,jobs"}). Treating each combination as a category would
produce 4\,547 mostly-singleton levels, so the field is tokenised on commas and
TF-IDF weighted over the 144 atomic tags, which keeps it dense enough to be
useful.

Speaker identity deserves a note, because it might look like the same kind of
shortcut as the credit-history columns. It is not. The speaker's name is
observable at prediction time, and one-hot encoding it lets a linear model learn
a per-speaker intercept from training rows only --- the same information that
the history features carry in aggregated form, expressed as an identity. Where
it does become a shortcut is in combination with the shipped counts, which is
precisely the combination we have removed.

\subsection{Feature Modes and Metadata Variants}

Three feature modes isolate where the signal lives:
\emph{text only} (word, and optionally character, TF-IDF);
\emph{metadata only} (numeric, one-hot and subject blocks);
and \emph{hybrid} (all blocks). The comparison is only meaningful once the
history features are leak-free --- with the shipped columns, ``metadata only''
would be measuring the leak.

Within the metadata blocks, four nested variants are treated as a modelling
choice rather than fixed: \texttt{base} uses party and state;
\texttt{speaker} adds speaker identity; \texttt{speaker\_subject} adds the
subject tags; and \texttt{all\_meta} adds job title and context. Combined with
the binary character-n-gram switch, this defines the search space of
Section 4.7.

\subsection{Classifiers}

Six classical classifiers span the usual families. All are
\texttt{scikit-learn} implementations\cite{pedregosa2011scikit} with a fixed
seed.

\textbf{Multinomial logistic regression} minimises the regularised
cross-entropy $\sum_i -\log \hat{p}(y_i \mid \bs{x}_i) + \tfrac{1}{2C}
\|\bs{W}\|_F^2$ with L-BFGS, giving calibrated posteriors over the six classes.

\textbf{Linear SVM} minimises the squared hinge loss in a one-versus-rest
arrangement\cite{cortes1995support}; scores are converted to pseudo-posteriors
by a softmax over decision values when probabilities are needed.

\textbf{SGD classifier} optimises the same family of linear objectives by
stochastic gradient descent under a modified-Huber or log loss, included because
it behaves differently from batch solvers on very sparse high-dimensional input.

\textbf{Multinomial naive Bayes}\cite{mccallum1998comparison} models each class
as a multinomial over feature counts with Laplace smoothing. It requires
non-negative input, so the pipeline clips negative entries to zero before
fitting. This is worth stating plainly: under naive Bayes the $z$-scored numeric
features are effectively rectified, so the model sees only the above-average
half of each history proportion. It is nonetheless the strongest hybrid model in
our results, which we take as evidence that the coarse direction of the history
signal, rather than its precise magnitude, is what carries.

\textbf{Random forest}\cite{breiman2001random} and \textbf{extremely randomised
trees}\cite{geurts2006extremely} are included as the non-linear members of the
bank, and because tree ensembles are exactly the models that exploit the leak of
Section 3 most aggressively --- a useful property for a diagnostic and a
liability for a benchmark.

\subsection{Selection Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

Reported test numbers are uninterpretable without knowing how much searching
produced them\cite{dodge2019show}, so the protocol is fixed in advance and
stated here in full.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The search space is the product of feature mode, metadata variant,
  character-n-gram switch, and per-model hyperparameter grid: 476
  configurations per task (Table~\ref{tab:grid}).
\item Every configuration is fitted on the training split and scored on the
  \emph{validation} split. The test split is not read at this stage.
\item The best configuration per (feature mode, model) cell by validation
  accuracy is carried forward --- 18 per task.
\item Those 18 are refitted on the training split and scored once on the test
  split. No configuration is revisited afterwards.
\end{enumerate}

Validation accuracy is reported alongside test accuracy in Section 7.4 only to
document the protocol. It is optimistically biased by the size of the search and
should not be read as a performance estimate; the gap between the two columns is
itself informative, and we discuss it in Section 8.2.

Separately from the search, a \emph{default configuration} --- the fixed
hyperparameters in \texttt{configs/baseline\_config.yaml}, party and state as
the only one-hot fields, no character n-grams --- is run across all six
(task, feature mode) cells. This is the ablation grid of Sections 7.2 and 7.3.
It involves no selection at all, so its test numbers carry no selection bias,
at the cost of not being tuned.

\subsection{Metrics}

Let $C$ be the number of classes and $\text{TP}_c, \text{FP}_c, \text{FN}_c$ the
per-class counts. We report accuracy, the unweighted mean of per-class F1,
\begin{equation}
\text{F1}_{\text{macro}} = \frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}
 \frac{2\,\text{TP}_c}{2\,\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c + \text{FN}_c},
\end{equation}
and the support-weighted mean of the same quantity. Macro-F1 is computed over
all classes on both tasks, so a column labelled ``macro'' means the same thing
everywhere; the positive-class F1 of the binary task is reported separately
rather than overwriting the macro column. This is a small point of hygiene, but
binary macro-F1 and positive-class F1 differ by up to eight points in our
results and are easy to confuse across papers.

Because the test split has $n = 1283$ rows, an accuracy estimate carries a
95\% Wilson interval\cite{wilson1927probable} of roughly $\pm 0.025$ at
$p \approx 0.28$ and $\pm 0.026$ at $p \approx 0.65$. Differences smaller than
about two and a half points are therefore not resolvable on this split, and we
avoid claiming them. This is a constraint of the benchmark, not of the models:
LIAR's test split is simply not large enough to separate systems that differ by
one point, which is worth remembering when reading a leaderboard whose entries
are spaced that closely.

\subsection{Implementation and Reproducibility}

The pipeline is implemented in Python 3.9 with \texttt{scikit-learn}
1.3.2\cite{pedregosa2011scikit}, \texttt{pandas} 2.1.4 and \texttt{numpy} 1.25.2.
All randomness --- fold assignment, tree construction, SGD shuffling --- is
seeded at 42. Every number in this paper is produced by one of five scripts:
\texttt{prepare\_data.py} (processed splits), \texttt{leakage\_analysis.py}
(Section 3), \texttt{train\_baselines.py} (Sections 7.2--7.3),
\texttt{tune\_baselines.py} with \texttt{evaluate\_final.py} (Section 7.4), and
\texttt{make\_figures.py} (all figures). A regression test in the accompanying
test suite asserts that no shipped \texttt{*\_c} column ever reaches a model's
feature matrix, so the correction cannot be undone silently by a later change.

The six default-configuration cells (two tasks by three feature modes, six
models each) run in about two minutes on a single CPU core, and the 476-configuration search takes roughly a quarter of an hour per
task. No GPU is required at any point, which is deliberate: a corrected baseline
is only useful if it is cheap enough that nobody is tempted to skip re-running
it.
%% ===========================================================================
\section{Experimental Setup}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Tasks, Splits and Targets}

Two task granularities are evaluated on the official splits of
Table~\ref{tab:splits}: the six-way ordinal task, treated as flat multi-class
classification, and the binary collapse defined in Section 4.2. The six-way task
is the one the dataset was built for and the one we care about; the binary task
is reported because it is what much of the literature quotes, and because a
pipeline that cannot beat 0.5666 on the easy task has nothing to say about the
hard one.

\subsection{Search Space}

Table~\ref{tab:grid} gives the full search space. It contains 476
configurations per task: 14 (feature mode, metadata variant, character-n-gram)
combinations $\times$ 34 model-hyperparameter points. Metadata variants are
searched only when metadata is in play, and the character-n-gram switch only
when statement text is in play, so the product is smaller than it first appears.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Search space, 476 configurations per task}
\label{tab:grid}
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Axis & Values \\
\midrule
Feature mode & text only, metadata only, hybrid \\
Metadata variant & \texttt{base}, \texttt{speaker},
                   \texttt{speaker\_subject}, \texttt{all\_meta} \\
Char n-grams & on, off \\
\midrule
Logistic regression & $C \in \{0.1, 0.5, 1, 3\}$; \\
                    & class weight $\in \{$none, balanced$\}$ \\
Linear SVM & $C \in \{0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5\}$; \\
           & class weight $\in \{$none, balanced$\}$ \\
SGD        & $\alpha \in \{10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\}$; \\
           & loss $\in \{$modified Huber, log$\}$ \\
Multinomial NB & $\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.5, 1, 2\}$ \\
Random forest  & 300 trees; depth $\in \{\infty, 30\}$; \\
               & min.\ leaf $\in \{1,3\}$ \\
Extra trees    & 300 trees; depth $\in \{\infty, 30\}$; \\
               & min.\ leaf $\in \{1,3\}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: the default configuration used for the ablation grid of
Sections 7.2--7.3 is not part of this search; it fixes $C = 1$, $\alpha = 1$,
100 trees at depth 25, the \texttt{base} metadata variant and no character
n-grams.}
\end{table}

\subsection{Reference Points}

Three reference points frame every result. The \textbf{majority-class} rate is
0.2081 on the six-way task and 0.5666 on the binary task. The \textbf{published
hybrid CNN} of the dataset paper reaches 0.274 six-way\cite{wang2017liar}, the
most directly comparable prior number since it uses statement text plus
metadata and the same splits. The \textbf{leaking constructions} of Section 3
--- 0.3944 raw and 0.6594 after the naive repair --- are included in plots as a
reminder of the scale of the artefact, never as baselines to beat.

\subsection{Compute}

All experiments run on a single CPU core. One (task, feature mode) cell of six
default models takes about 21 seconds end to end, so the entire six-cell
ablation grid completes in roughly two minutes; the 952-configuration search
across both tasks is the expensive part, dominated by the 300-tree ensembles on
character-n-gram matrices. No GPU is used anywhere in this paper.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Exploratory Analysis}
%% ===========================================================================

This section documents the properties of the corpus that shaped the design
choices above. It is deliberately placed after the method, because several of
the observations only make sense once the distinction between the shipped
columns and the reconstructed ones is on the table.

\subsection{Missingness}

Fig.~\ref{fig:missing} shows missingness per column over the combined corpus.
Two fields stand out: \texttt{job\_title} is absent for 27.86\% of rows and
\texttt{state} for 21.46\%, with \texttt{context} missing for 1.00\% and
nothing else missing at all. The pattern is structural rather than accidental.
Speakers who are organisations, media outlets, chain emails or viral social
posts have no formal job title and no home state, and roughly a quarter of LIAR
consists of exactly such speakers. This is why those fields are imputed with an
explicit \texttt{"Unknown"} level rather than dropped: the absence is itself a
speaker-type signal, and discarding the rows would remove a quarter of the
corpus to fix a field that only two of our four metadata variants even use.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_missing.pdf}
\caption{Missingness per column over all 12\,836 statements. Columns not shown
have no missing values}
\label{fig:missing}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Label Distribution}

Fig.~\ref{fig:labels} gives the label distribution per split.
Five of the six classes sit between 16\% and 21\%; \emph{pants-fire} is the
outlier at 8.18\%. The three splits are close to one another, with the largest
discrepancy in \emph{pants-fire} (8.20\% of train, 9.03\% of validation, 7.17\%
of test) and in \emph{true} (16.39\%, 13.16\%, 16.45\%). The validation split
is thus slightly harder-leaning than the test split, which shows up later as a
systematic gap between validation and test accuracy on the binary task
(Section 7.4).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_labels.pdf}
\caption{Label distribution as a share of each split. The splits are close to
one another, with \emph{pants-fire} the only strongly under-represented class}
\label{fig:labels}
\end{figure}

The practical consequence for modelling is a benign one: no class is rare enough
to require resampling, and none is common enough for a trivial classifier to
score well. But it also means the six-way task has very little headroom above
0.2081, so an absolute accuracy of 0.284 --- unimpressive-looking on its face
--- is a 36\% relative improvement over the trivial baseline.

\subsection{Statement Surface Statistics}

Statements are short and uniform. Character length averages 106.4 (standard
deviation 45.0, median 99, range 11--395), word count averages 17.9 (standard
deviation 7.8, median 17, range 2--66), and mean word length is tightly
concentrated at 6.00 characters (standard deviation 0.69). There is no long tail
of documents: the longest statement in the corpus is under four hundred
characters. Two design consequences follow. First, the 512-token limit of a
standard transformer encoder is irrelevant on this corpus, so the advantage of
large models here is representational rather than a matter of context length.
Second, with eighteen words per document and a 5\,000-term vocabulary, the
word-level TF-IDF matrix averages only 10.3 non-zeros per row, which is why
character n-grams --- which produce a much denser representation --- help as
much as they do in Section 7.4.

\subsection{Speaker Structure}

The corpus contains 3\,318 distinct speakers, and the distribution over them is
extremely uneven: 2\,056 statements come from speakers with exactly one
statement in the entire corpus, while the most heavily fact-checked figures
account for hundreds each. Fig.~\ref{fig:history}(b) shows the distribution of
out-of-fold history support over training rows. Of test statements, 84.4\% come
from a speaker who also appears in training; the remaining 15.6\% have no
usable history at all and fall back to the corpus prior by construction
(Equation~(\ref{eq:smooth})). The corresponding figure for validation is 17.2\%
and, under out-of-fold encoding, 20.2\% for training rows themselves.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{figures/fig_history.pdf}
\caption{(a) Mean leak-free credibility score by true label on the test split,
with standard errors; the ordering is monotone across all six levels.
(b) Distribution of out-of-fold speaker history support over training rows,
on a logarithmic scale}
\label{fig:history}
\end{figure*}

This unevenness is exactly why smoothing matters. Without it, a speaker with one
prior statement would receive a saturated one-hot proportion vector,
indistinguishable in form from a speaker with four hundred statements and a
genuinely concentrated record --- and, as Section 3.2 showed, saturated vectors
of that kind are what a tree ensemble memorises.

\subsection{Does the Corrected History Carry Any Signal?}

Fig.~\ref{fig:history}(a) answers the obvious question about the corrected
features: having removed the leak, is anything left? Mean credibility score on
the test split increases monotonically across the six labels, from $-0.61$ for
\emph{pants-fire} through $-0.28$ (\emph{false}), $-0.22$
(\emph{barely-true}), $-0.10$ (\emph{half-true}) and $-0.09$
(\emph{mostly-true}) to $-0.07$ for \emph{true}. The ordering is correct and the
separation at the extremes is clear, but the four upper classes are separated by
hundredths of a point with overlapping standard errors. That shape --- a real
signal that distinguishes fabrications from everything else, and almost nothing
that distinguishes \emph{half-true} from \emph{mostly-true} --- predicts the
confusion structure we observe in Section 7.6.

\subsection{Correlation Structure of the Shipped Columns}

Fig.~\ref{fig:corr} shows the correlation matrix over the shipped count
columns, their sum, the three text statistics and the binary target. Three
things are visible. The five counts are strongly inter-correlated (0.16 to
0.99), because a speaker with a long fact-checking record accumulates counts in
every bucket at once --- which is why the total, not the composition, dominates
their variance. The text statistics are essentially uncorrelated with all of
them ($|r| < 0.05$), confirming that the two blocks carry independent
information. And the binary target correlates only weakly with any single count
($|r| \le 0.16$, strongest for \texttt{pants\_fire\_c}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figures/fig_corr.pdf}
\caption{Correlation matrix over the shipped credit-history columns, their sum,
the statement surface statistics and the binary target. Low correlation between
the text block and the history block indicates independent signal}
\label{fig:corr}
\end{figure}

That last observation is worth dwelling on, because it is a trap. A correlation
of $-0.16$ between \texttt{pants\_fire\_c} and the binary target looks like a
weak feature, and a modeller doing univariate screening would reasonably keep it
without concern. Yet the same five columns support a 0.3944 six-way classifier.
The leak is invisible to marginal correlation analysis because it lives in the
\emph{joint} structure --- in the fact that the vector identifies the speaker
and, for sparse speakers, the row's own label. Feature screening by correlation
would not have caught it; only asking where the numbers came from did.
%% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
%% ===========================================================================

Results are presented in three layers. Section 7.1 restates the audit as a
result in its own right. Sections 7.2 and 7.3 give the untuned ablation grid,
where no selection of any kind takes place and the test numbers are therefore
free of selection bias. Section 7.4 gives the tuned results under the protocol
of Section 4.7. Sections 7.5 to 7.9 analyse what the numbers mean.

\subsection{The Corrected Signal in Speaker History}

Table~\ref{tab:effect} established the headline correction, and it is worth
restating as a result: the shipped credit-history columns support a 0.3944
six-way classifier, the naive repair a 0.6594 one, and the leakage-free
reconstruction a 0.2284 one against a 0.2081 majority rate. The corrected
history-only model clears the trivial baseline by 2.0 points, an interval that
does not quite separate from zero on a 1\,283-row split
(95\% Wilson intervals $[0.206, 0.252]$ and $[0.187, 0.231]$ overlap). Speaker
history, used honestly, is a weak feature on its own. Its value appears in
combination, which is what the next two subsections measure.

\subsection{Ablation Grid: Six-Class Task}

Table~\ref{tab:6class} gives test accuracy and macro-F1 for all six classifiers
under all three feature modes, using the default configuration --- fixed
hyperparameters, no search, so nothing here is selected on anything.

feature mode}
\label{tab:6class}

\cmidrule(lr){2-4}\cmidrule(lr){5-7}
Model & Text & Meta & Hyb. & Text & Meta & Hyb. \\
\midrule
Multinomial NB      & .2393 & .2362 & \best{.2837} & .1984 & .2351 & \best{.2773} \\
Logistic regression & .2432 & .2751 & .2611 & .2151 & .2704 & .2557 \\
Linear SVM          & .2369 & .2712 & .2424 & .2260 & .2663 & .2425 \\
Extra trees         & .2175 & .2416 & .2588 & .1335 & .2329 & .2186 \\
Random forest       & .2065 & .2440 & .2502 & .1327 & .2349 & .2106 \\
SGD                 & .2354 & .2229 & .2330 & .2235 & .2204 & .2320 \\
\midrule
Majority class      & \multicolumn{3}{c}{.2081} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{---} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: Text = word TF-IDF only; Meta = numeric, one-hot and
subject blocks only; Hyb.\ = both. Best value per metric in bold. All numbers
use fixed default hyperparameters with no search.}
\end{table}

Four observations follow.

\textbf{Every feature mode beats the majority class, but not by much.} The best
cell is 0.2837, 7.6 points above the trivial baseline, which is the honest
headline number for a classical model on six-way LIAR. The weakest text-only
tree ensembles (0.2065) do not beat it at all.

\textbf{Metadata alone is at least as strong as text alone.} Logistic regression
reaches 0.2751 on metadata against 0.2432 on text, and linear SVM 0.2712 against
0.2369. Eighteen words of political speech carry less about veracity than the
identity, party and topic of the speaker --- which is intuitive, and which is
precisely why the integrity of the metadata matters so much on this benchmark.

\textbf{Hybrid wins, but only for some models.} Multinomial naive Bayes gains
4.4 points from the combination (0.2393 text, 0.2362 metadata, 0.2837 hybrid) and
the tree ensembles gain as well, whereas the linear models are \emph{worse}
hybrid than metadata-only (logistic regression 0.2611 against 0.2751). The
5\,000 sparse text columns dilute the twelve dense numeric ones under a single
L2 penalty; naive Bayes, which treats each feature independently, does not
suffer that dilution. This is a representation-balancing problem rather than an
information problem, and it is the clearest place where a better model family
would help.

\textbf{Macro-F1 separates the models more sharply than accuracy.} The tree
ensembles lose 8 points of macro-F1 relative to their accuracy under text-only
features (0.2175 accuracy against 0.1335 macro-F1 for extra trees), meaning they
concentrate predictions on the larger classes and abandon \emph{pants-fire}
entirely. Naive Bayes retains a macro-F1 within 0.6 points of its accuracy,
which on a six-way ordinal task is the more useful behaviour.

and 0.735, well above macro-F1, which is the asymmetry we warned about in

Val is reported to document the protocol, not as a performance estimate.}
\end{table}

Three things are worth reading off this table.

\textbf{The modality ordering survives tuning.} On both tasks the ordering is
hybrid $>$ metadata $>$ text, exactly as in the untuned grid, with the hybrid
margin over text at 1.4 points on the six-class task and 4.6 on the binary task
--- essentially unchanged from the untuned grid. The conclusion of Section 7.5
therefore does not depend on the hyperparameters being the defaults.

\textbf{Tuning buys almost nothing on the six-class task.} The best untuned cell
reached 0.2837; 476 configurations per task and a metadata-variant search
produced 0.2845, an improvement of 0.08 points --- roughly a thirtieth of the
Wilson interval. On the binary task the gain is larger but still modest: 0.6610
to 0.6726, 1.2 points. Whatever is limiting these models, it is not
hyperparameter choice.

\textbf{The search does select structure, just not much performance.} Character
n-grams are chosen in 10 of the 12 cells where statement text is in play on the
six-class task, and in all 12 on the binary task; the speaker-identity variants
(\texttt{spk}, \texttt{spk+sbj}) win 8 of the 12 cells where metadata is in play
on the six-class task and 7 of 12 on the binary task. Both choices are
consistent with the qualitative picture: sub-word features help on very short
documents, and knowing who is speaking helps more than any hyperparameter does.

The validation column also shows the two directions in which a validation
estimate can mislead. On the six-class task validation over-estimates test by
1.7 points on average, and by 2.4 points in the hybrid mode --- the expected
optimistic bias from searching. On the binary task the average gap almost
vanishes (0.25 points) and reverses in the hybrid mode, where validation
\emph{under}-estimates test by 0.22 points: LIAR's validation split has a lower
true-leaning rate (0.5202) than its test split (0.5666) and is simply the harder
of the two, and that difference roughly cancels the optimistic bias. Neither
direction is a defect of the protocol; both are reasons not to quote a
validation number as a result.

\subsection{Where the Hybrid Gain Comes From}

The modality ablation answers a question the leak had previously made
unanswerable: how much does speaker context actually add once it is computed
honestly? Taking the best model per cell of the untuned grid, the six-class task
improves from
0.2432 (text) and 0.2751 (metadata) to 0.2837 (hybrid), and the binary task from
0.6142 and 0.6485 to 0.6610. The hybrid gain over the better single modality is
therefore 0.9 points on the six-class task and 1.3 on the binary task --- real,
consistent in sign across both tasks and most models, and smaller than the
Wilson interval of either estimate taken alone.

That last clause deserves emphasis rather than burial. On a 1\,283-row test
split, a one-point improvement is not statistically resolvable. What makes the
hybrid result credible is not its margin on any single cell but its
\emph{consistency}: hybrid is the best or second-best mode for every model on
both tasks, and it produces the best overall cell on both. A single cell would
prove nothing; twelve model-task combinations pointing the same way is weak but
genuine evidence.

The contrast with the leaking construction is the point of the exercise. With
the shipped columns, metadata-only would have reported roughly 0.39 on the
six-class task and text would have looked worthless by comparison --- a
conclusion that is exactly backwards. Corrected, the two modalities sit within
three or four points of one another, and their combination adds about one more.

Label & Precision & Recall & F1 & Support \\
\midrule
\emph{pants-fire}  & 0.400 & 0.261 & 0.316 & 92 \\
\emph{false}       & 0.285 & 0.404 & 0.334 & 250 \\
\emph{barely-true} & 0.289 & 0.131 & 0.180 & 214 \\
\emph{half-true}   & 0.279 & 0.318 & 0.297 & 267 \\
\emph{mostly-true} & 0.260 & 0.321 & 0.287 & 249 \\
