\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize Note: overall accuracy 0.2837. \emph{pants-fire} has the highest
precision of any class despite being the rarest, and \emph{barely-true} the
lowest recall of any class.}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{figures/fig_confusion.pdf}
\caption{Row-normalised confusion matrix for the six-class hybrid multinomial
naive Bayes classifier on the test split. Mass concentrates near the diagonal
band rather than on the diagonal itself}
\label{fig:confusion}
\end{figure}

Two structural facts emerge.

\textbf{The extremes are easier than the middle.} \emph{Pants-fire} achieves the
highest precision of any class (0.400) despite having the smallest support, and
\emph{false} the highest F1 (0.334). \emph{Barely-true} is nearly invisible to
the model, with 0.131 recall: it sits between \emph{false} and \emph{half-true}
on the scale and is absorbed by both. This mirrors the credibility-score profile
of Fig.~\ref{fig:history}(a) exactly --- history separates fabrications from
everything else and says almost nothing about the middle of the scale --- and it
is the most useful qualitative finding in the paper. The model is not uniformly
weak; it is competent at the end of the scale that matters most operationally
(identifying outright fabrications) and helpless in the middle.

\textbf{Errors are ordinal, not arbitrary.} Exact accuracy is 0.2837, but 0.6321
of predictions fall within one level of the true label and 0.8223 within two.
A classifier drawing predictions independently from the same marginal
distribution would score 0.1862 exactly and 0.4909 within one level, so both the
exact and the near-miss rates carry information. The mean absolute ordinal error
is 1.35 levels. The model has learned the \emph{direction} of
truthfulness without resolving its granularity --- which suggests that treating
the task as flat multi-class classification, as we and most of the literature
do, discards usable structure. An ordinal or regression formulation with a
threshold-based decoder is an obvious next step, and one that costs nothing in
model capacity.

For the binary task, the best configuration reaches 0.661 accuracy with
precision 0.624 and recall 0.547 on the false-leaning class against precision
0.683 and recall 0.748 on the true-leaning class. The asymmetry is consistent
with the six-class picture: the model over-predicts the majority (true-leaning)
side, and the errors it makes on the minority side are the barely-true and
half-true statements that sit closest to the decision boundary.

\subsection{Qualitative Error Analysis}

Inspecting the model's most confident predictions is unusually informative here,
because they are all the same speaker. The four highest-confidence correct
predictions and the four highest-confidence errors on the six-class test split
all belong to \texttt{chain-email}, LIAR's catch-all speaker for anonymous
forwarded messages, which has 142 training statements of which 82 are
\emph{pants-fire} and 34 \emph{false}. Its corrected credibility score is
$-2.03$ on a scale whose floor is $-3$.

The model's behaviour follows directly: it predicts \emph{pants-fire} for all
thirteen \texttt{chain-email} statements in the test split, at confidence above
0.99 for several of them. Six are correct. The remaining seven are not, and two
of those are labelled \emph{true} --- including the claim that a president had
``visited more countries and met with more world leaders than any president in
his first six months in office'', which PolitiFact rated true and the model
rated a fabrication with confidence 1.00. A 46\% accuracy on this speaker is far
above the model's 28\% overall, so the speaker prior is earning its place; but
it is doing so by refusing to read the statement.

This is the failure mode a metadata-heavy model has on this corpus, and it is
worth naming precisely. Speaker history is predictive because sources are
consistent, which means a model that leans on it will be confidently wrong
exactly when a usually-unreliable source happens to say something true. For a
deployed fact-checking aid, that is the expensive error: it is the case where
automation would suppress a true statement from a distrusted source.

The complementary measurement is cold start. On the 200 test statements from
speakers with no training history, accuracy is 0.240; on the 1\,083 with
history, it is 0.2918. The 5.2-point gap is a direct measure of what speaker
history contributes, and it is consistent with the history-only result of
Section 7.1. It also sets an upper bound on how much a speaker-graph model can
help without external information: on a sixth of the test split there is no
speaker signal to propagate.

\subsection{Comparison with Published Results}

Table~\ref{tab:positioning} placed our numbers alongside published ones, and the
comparison needs care in both directions.

Our corrected classical numbers are \emph{below} every published neural result
on this benchmark, which is the expected outcome and not a finding: a TF-IDF
model with twelve numeric features should not match a fine-tuned DeBERTa. The
appropriate comparison for our 0.2837 is the 0.274 of the original hybrid
CNN\cite{wang2017liar}, which our best configuration matches within the
resolution of the split.

The reverse comparison is the one that matters. We cannot determine which
published systems consumed the credit-history columns as distributed, because
most papers reporting metadata gains on LIAR do not say. What the audit
establishes is a lower bound on the concern: any system that fed those five
columns into a model with the capacity to memorise 392 distinct vectors was
given, for 16\% of rows, a direct encoding of the answer, and for a further
large fraction, a summary that includes the row's own label. A reported gain
from metadata on LIAR is therefore not interpretable without a statement of how
those columns were handled. We suggest that such a statement become routine, in
the same way that reporting a random seed did.

\subsection{Stability}

Two checks bound how much of the above depends on arbitrary choices. First,
hybrid features rank first or second for all six model families on both tasks,
so the modality conclusion does not rest on a particular classifier; the
metadata-over-text ordering is weaker, holding clearly for the two linear
margin-based models and reversing slightly for naive Bayes and SGD. Second, the untuned and tuned
protocols agree on the qualitative conclusions --- the same feature-mode
ordering, the same best task margin --- while differing by one to two points in
absolute terms, so the conclusions do not depend on the search either. What we
have not done is resample the splits; as Gorman and
Bedrick\cite{gorman2019standard} show, conclusions from a single standard split
can fail to replicate, and every number here is conditioned on LIAR's official
partition. We keep that partition because it is the only way to remain
comparable with the literature, and we flag the limitation in Section 8.5
rather than pretending it away.
%% ===========================================================================
\section{Discussion}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{What the Leak Means for Work on LIAR}

The audit does not say that published results on LIAR are wrong. It says that a
particular set of five columns cannot be used as distributed, and that a paper
which uses them owes its readers an account of how. The distinction matters.
Text-only results on LIAR are untouched by this finding. Results that use party,
state, subject or speaker identity are untouched. Only results that consume the
\texttt{*\_c} columns are implicated, and the size of the implication depends on
the model: a linear model over five weakly-correlated integers extracts far less
from the leak than a depth-25 forest, which is why our diagnostic used the
forest.

What the finding does change is how a metadata gain should be read. Before the
audit, a paper reporting that metadata improved LIAR accuracy by ten points was
reporting something ambiguous between two very different claims: that speaker
context helps, or that the model found the answer key. Our corrected measurement
puts a number on the honest version of the first claim --- about one accuracy
point over the better single modality, for classical models --- which is a
useful calibration for anyone interpreting a larger reported gain.

There is also a broader point about benchmark hygiene. This leak survived eight
years and hundreds of citations, not because it is subtle in retrospect, but
because nothing in a standard workflow would surface it. The columns have
plausible names, plausible magnitudes, and unremarkable marginal correlations
with the target (Section 6.6). They fail only under a question that no automated
check asks: \emph{when was this number computed, relative to the label?}
Kaufman \emph{et al.}\cite{kaufman2012leakage} predicted exactly this failure
mode --- leakage found through implausibly good results rather than through
inspection --- and the recommendation that follows is procedural: for any
label-derived feature shipped with a dataset, reconstruct it from the raw labels
and check that you get the same numbers. Here, you do not.

\subsection{What the Search Buys}

Section 7.4 reported an uncomfortable number: 476 configurations per task,
searched over feature variants, character n-grams and hyperparameters, improved
six-class test accuracy from 0.2837 to 0.2845. Eight hundredths of a point. On
the binary task the return was larger --- 1.2 points --- but still inside the
interval. It is worth asking what that means, because a great deal of effort in
this literature goes into search.

The first reading is the obvious one: these models are limited by their features
and their hypothesis class, not by their settings. That is consistent with
everything else in the paper. The second reading is more interesting, and it
concerns whether validation accuracy is even a useful ranking signal at this
resolution. Across all 18 selected cells per task, the Spearman correlation
between validation and test accuracy is 0.81 on the six-class task and 0.83 on
the binary task, which looks reassuring. But that correlation is carried almost
entirely by the gap \emph{between} feature modes --- text-only configurations
are worse on both splits, so they drag the rank correlation up. Restricted to
the six hybrid configurations, where the differences are small and the choice
actually matters, the correlation is $-0.67$ on the six-class task and $-0.41$
on the binary task. It is negative.

Concretely: the configuration with the highest validation accuracy on the
six-class task (a 300-tree random forest, 0.3069 validation) scores 0.2736 on
test, while the configuration ranked fifth on validation (SGD, 0.2975) scores
the best test result of 0.2845. The same pattern holds on the binary task, where
the validation winner scores 0.6493 against the best test result of 0.6726.

The honest conclusion is that on a 1\,284-row validation split, selecting among
closely-matched configurations is close to a coin flip, and the winner of such a
search is partly a winner by luck. This is precisely what Dodge \emph{et
al.}\cite{dodge2019show} argue when they ask for search budgets to be reported
alongside results, and it is a good reason to prefer the untuned grid of
Sections 7.2 and 7.3 as the paper's reference numbers: they involve no selection
at all, and they are within a point of the tuned ones.

\subsection{Why Classical Models Plateau Here}

Three limits are visible in our results, and they are worth separating because
only one of them is about model capacity.

\textbf{The signal in the metadata is genuinely thin.} Corrected speaker history
supports 0.2284 on its own against a 0.2081 baseline. No architecture recovers
information that is not in the features; a graph neural network over speakers
and parties is operating on the same underlying signal we measured, differently
encoded.

\textbf{The text is short and the label depends on external facts.} An eighteen
word statement about a budget figure is true or false because of the budget, not
because of its wording. No model that sees only the sentence can resolve that,
which is the ceiling every text-only approach on LIAR runs into, and it explains
why retrieval-augmented and evidence-conditioned systems --- including the
justification-based approach of Alhindi \emph{et
al.}\cite{alhindi2018where} --- show the largest jumps. The honest version of
that observation is that LIAR without evidence retrieval is closer to a speaker
profiling task than a fact-checking task.

\textbf{The representation is poorly balanced.} Section 7.2 showed linear models
losing accuracy when 5\,000 sparse text columns are concatenated with twelve
dense numeric ones under a single penalty. This one \emph{is} a modelling
limitation rather than an information limitation, and it is the most
straightforward thing to fix: separate regularisation per block, a learned gate
between modalities, or a late-fusion ensemble would all address it. That such a
basic representational issue costs more accuracy than the entire corrected
metadata signal is a useful reminder of where effort is best spent.

\subsection{Recommendations for Future Work on LIAR}

We suggest five concrete practices.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Do not use the \texttt{*\_c} columns as features.} They are
  self-including and cross-split aggregating. If you want speaker history, build
  it from training labels, out-of-fold, as in Section 4.3.
\item \textbf{Do not repair them by subtracting the row's own label.} By
  Proposition~\ref{prop:naive} this makes the leak worse, and it does so while
  looking like a fix --- the most dangerous combination.
\item \textbf{State how metadata was handled.} A single sentence --- ``the
  shipped credit-history columns were excluded'' or ``were used as provided''
  --- makes a reported metadata gain interpretable. Without it, it is not.
\item \textbf{Report macro-F1 and say what it averages over.} Binary macro-F1
  and positive-class F1 differ by up to nineteen points in our results, and both
  are routinely labelled ``F1''.
\item \textbf{Quote the size of the search alongside the test
  number}\cite{dodge2019show}, and remember that the 1\,283-row test split
  resolves differences of about two and a half accuracy points at best. Ranked
  tables whose entries are spaced more closely than that are reporting noise.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Threats to Validity}

\textbf{Single split.} Every number is conditioned on LIAR's official
partition. Gorman and Bedrick\cite{gorman2019standard} show that conclusions
drawn this way frequently fail to replicate under resampling. We keep the
official split for comparability, but the modality ordering in particular should
be regarded as provisional until it is checked under repeated random splits.

\textbf{Interval width.} At $n = 1283$, 95\% Wilson intervals are roughly
$\pm 2.5$ points. The 0.9-point hybrid gain on the six-class task is therefore
supported by consistency across twelve model-task combinations rather than by
any single
comparison, and we have tried not to overstate it.

\textbf{Classical models only.} We deliberately did not add a transformer or a
graph model, so we cannot say how much of the corrected-metadata signal a
stronger encoder would extract. It is possible --- we would say likely --- that
a model able to condition text on speaker identity recovers more from the same
features than a linear combination does.

\textbf{The audit is of one corpus.} We measured LIAR. We have not checked
whether comparable columns in other fact-checking corpora are constructed the
same way, though the pattern --- a per-entity aggregate computed once over a
whole corpus and broadcast to rows --- is common enough that it would be worth
checking.

\textbf{Encoding asymmetry.} Training rows see roughly 80\% of the available
speaker history and held-out rows see all of it (Section 4.3). We expose the
support explicitly so a model can condition on it, but the asymmetry is real and
slightly favours held-out rows.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusions}
%% ===========================================================================

The five credit-history columns distributed with LIAR are not a summary of a
speaker's past. They are a summary of the speaker's record across the entire
corpus, copied onto every row, and they therefore contain both the row's own
label and the labels of the held-out splits. We quantified this: the vector is
constant for 3\,314 of 3\,318 speakers, matches the full-corpus tally for 2\,846
of 2\,947, and one-hot encodes the row's own label for 1\,689 of 1\,701
single-statement speakers. A random forest given nothing else reaches 0.3944
six-class test accuracy, and the natural repair of subtracting the row's own
label raises that to 0.6594 rather than lowering it --- because subtracting a
label from a constant, memorisable aggregate turns the feature vector into a
displacement whose direction is the label.

Rebuilt from training labels only, out-of-fold, and smoothed toward the corpus
prior, the same signal supports 0.2284 --- two points above the majority class
rather than nineteen. On that corrected footing, six classical classifiers over
three feature modes and two task granularities give a clean set of reference
numbers: 0.2837 six-class and 0.6610 binary test accuracy without any tuning,
and 0.2845 and 0.6726 under a protocol that searches 476 configurations per
task on validation and scores test once. The hybrid feature set ranks first or second for every model on both
tasks, and speaker context contributes about one accuracy point over the better
single modality --- real, consistent, and an order of magnitude smaller than the
leak it replaces.

The per-class analysis suggests where the remaining signal is. Fabrications are
the most separable class (0.400 precision on the rarest label), the middle of
the scale is nearly indistinguishable (0.131 recall on \emph{barely-true}), and
63\% of predictions land within one level of the truth against 49\% by chance.
The model learns the direction of truthfulness without its granularity.

\textbf{Future work.} Three extensions follow directly. First, an ordinal
formulation --- cumulative-link or regression with learned thresholds --- to
exploit the near-miss structure the confusion matrix reveals. Second, a
transformer encoder over the statement, fused with the corrected history
features through a per-block gate rather than plain concatenation, which
addresses the representation-balancing failure of Section 8.3 directly. Third, a
speaker--subject graph model, which is the natural home for the relational
signal that our tabular encoding flattens. Any such extension must consume
speaker history through the out-of-fold encoder of Section 4.3; training on the
shipped columns reproduces the inflated numbers documented here, and those
numbers will look like progress.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Reproduction}
%% ===========================================================================

Every number, table and figure in this paper is regenerated by the following
sequence, run from the repository root with a fixed seed of 42.

\begin{quote}\footnotesize\ttfamily
\noindent
python scripts/prepare\_data.py\\[2pt]
python scripts/leakage\_analysis.py\\[2pt]
python scripts/train\_baselines.py \textbackslash\\
\hspace*{1em}--task \{6class,binary\} \textbackslash\\
\hspace*{1em}--feature-mode \{text\_only,\\
\hspace*{2em}metadata\_only,hybrid\}\\[2pt]
python scripts/tune\_baselines.py --task \{6class,binary\}\\[2pt]
python scripts/evaluate\_final.py --task \{6class,binary\}\\[2pt]
python scripts/summarize\_results.py\\[2pt]
python make\_figures.py\\[2pt]
pytest
\end{quote}

\noindent
The first command writes the processed splits, the second reproduces
Tables~\ref{tab:audit} and~\ref{tab:effect} together with the decodability
measurement of Section 3.5, the third is run once for each of the six
(task, feature mode) cells behind Tables~\ref{tab:6class}
and~\ref{tab:binary}, and the fourth and fifth implement the
selection protocol of Section 4.7. The test suite includes a regression test
asserting that no shipped \texttt{*\_c} column appears in any model feature set,
so the correction cannot be reverted silently.

Wall-clock times on a single CPU core: preparation and the leakage analysis
complete in well under a minute each; one (task, feature mode) cell of six
default models takes about 21 seconds; the 476-configuration search takes
roughly a quarter of an hour per task, dominated by 300-tree ensembles on
character-n-gram matrices.
